newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: All quiet in Serbian city under opposition rule.
newsitem.headline: All quiet in Serbian city under opposition rule.

text.p: While thousands demonstrate daily in Belgrade to force the government to reinstate November election results, it is all quiet in the city of Novi Sad, which is already under opposition rule.

"We had major demonstrations before the New Year, but now nobody is coming out," said Slobodan Tomic, a 21-year-old student at the Faculty of Technical Sciences in Novi Sad, a city of 300,000 on the Danube River 75 km (45 miles) north of Belgrade.
"In Belgrade the results (of November municipal elections) were close and we demonstrated to support the opposition, but there was no way anyone could claim fraud in Novi Sad."

Here candidates of the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition won a crushing victory in the elections, leaving Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's Socialist Party (SPS) with only six seats on the council.
Zajedno candidates also won 14 other cities, including Belgrade, but the government annulled those results, claiming irregularities and prompting the demonstrations now into their third month.
"It was just too big a victory (in Novi Sad) and they could not ignore such a big win," said Miodrag Vojnovic, 40, a lawyer. "In Belgrade the results were close and they tried to stop it."
Zajedno now has 39 seats on the town council, the rightist Serbian Radical Party nine, the SPS six and 16 held by minor parties.
But the opposition taking control of the city council has not brought an immediate end to Novi Sad's stark problems of high unemployment, low wages and underutilisation of factories.
"The economic situation here is not good," said Igor Pantic, 24, who runs a popular coffee house on the city's pedestrian mall.
"We have factories but they are not up to European standard. What we produce is very good but it is expensive and the Turks, Greeks and Italians make it cheaper," said Pantic.
He is so frustrated by the job market that he is thinking of emigrating to Australia.
Four years of sanctions which the international community slapped on Serbia during the war in Bosnia had a devastating effect on Novi Sad, and on the rest of Serbia.

The city's textile mills and metal factories work at a fraction of their capacity although food processing in the agriculturally rich Vojvodina, of which Novi Sad is the provincial capital, is one of the economy's growing sectors.
The city's new Zajedno-led government says that trying to remedy Novi Sad's problems is a frustrating experience.

"As far as unemployment is concerned, we can only deal with the social part of the problem because all the firms who have laid off workers are owned by the republic," deputy Mayor Predrag Filipov told Reuters, referring to Serbia's still largely state-run economy.
"The city has no authority in this sector. All it can do is stimulate part of the private sector," Filipov said.

Similarly, he said that of 1.5 billion dinars ($300 million at official exchange rate) paid in taxes by citizens of Novi Sad, only 67 million dinars ($13.4 million) is funnelled back after passing through the Socialist-run central government.
"We will call for autonomy in town earnings," Filipov said. "This will let the town keep a larger part of its earnings."
Whether a four-year mandate will be long enough for Zajedno to accomplish all it wants in Novi Sad remains to be seen, and will be closely scrutinised by local residents.
"If Zajedno doesn't improve the situation here in the next four years they must go," Pantic said. "But the biggest problem was getting the Socialists out. After that it will be easy."
